text.p: European stocks bounced back on Friday, encouraged by a strong overnight rally on Wall Street, and sterling surged to a six-year high against the mark, lured by the prospect of higher interest rates.

The dollar also strengthened against the mark as the impact of remarks by Germany's top central banker supporting the mark waned and traders focused on the likely reaction to German budget details due later on Friday.

The British pound vaulted over 2.98 marks for the first time since April 1991 as initial dismay that British interest rates rose by only a quarter-percentage point on Thursday gave way to expectations that more increases were on the way.

The prospect of a three-mark pound proved irresistible to short-term traders although longer-term investors were wary of piling in after a year-long rally which has boosted sterling 30 percent against the mark.
The pound rose as high as 2.9870 marks by mid-morning. It also climbed to $1.6980, its best showing since January 10.

"Traders are going for big levels like three against the mark and 1.70 against the dollar because the Bank of England has no choice but to raise rates," said Ian Winship, a fund manager at Scottish Amicable Investment Managers in Glasgow.
"But I'd rather not buy gilts or sterling for my overseas accounts right now as I'm too nervous about it swinging around."

Traders are betting on higher British interest rates to quell inflationary pressures, making sterling assets a more attractive investment. The pound also benefited from market wariness about the strength of a future European single currency.

The sterling rally against the mark helped to push the dollar up over half a pfennig against the German currency to levels it held before Thursday's retreat on mark-positive comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.
"The dollar's climb today is really all down to sterling/mark," said a U.S. bank analyst.

The impact of Tietmeyer's remarks on Thursday, in which he said he wanted to see a strong mark going into the single currency and that the dollar's correction against the mark was over, had waned by mid-morning.

"Tietmeyer's remarks gave the mark a boost but that has now faded," said Sonja Gibbs, market strategist at Nomura International. "Focus is on the contents of the German budget but this is unlikely to change the perception of a broad EMU."
The German cabinet said it approved the 1998 draft and 1997 supplementary budgets.
Frankfurt regained its form after dipping nearly two percent on Thursday to make hefty gains. Dealers said the market rally was likely to keep on rolling as conditions remained ideal.

"I can't think of any negative factors, we have the best of all possible scenarios for the share market," one Frankfurt share trader said. "My only slight fear is that people are piling into the stock market without really knowing what they are buying."
The strong dollar was helping Frankfurt's bull run as it improved prospects for the exporting sector. Investors' optimism was also encouraged by low interest rates and inflation-free growth.

The blue-chip DAX index touched 4,050.41 points by mid morning, a gain of 1.3 percent. Frankfurt closed at a record high earlier this week and dealers said the bourse was on course to reach 4,250 points.
London climbed nearly 0.5 percent after a dull performance on Thursday, lifted by Wall Street and a rally in retailing stocks.
"Wall Street should help us, but the main driving factor at the moment is the squeeze in the retail and food retail sectors," said one senior dealer.

New York stocks clawed back part of the previous day's big losses overnight as investors focused on corporate earnings, which have been mostly upbeat so far in the second-quarter reporting period. The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 44.33 points at 7,886.76.

In London, investors were still breathing a collective sigh of relief at the 25 basis-point interest rate hike but some were nervous that the relatively mild monetary tightening left open the possibility of another rate increase in early August.

In Paris, stocks made only modest advances in light trade ahead of the long Bastille Day holiday weekend. Eurotunnel fell back after touching a trading year high of 8.95 francs as shareholders massively backed the company's plan to restructure its 70 billion francs of debt.
